title: Continuous Practice
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley reads "Continuous Practice, How and Why," a talk Sojun Mel Weitsman gave on the sixth day of a Rohatsu sesshin, and comments on it. Mel holds that how to live this moment matters more than why, and that practice means keeping the mind in harmony with the heart. Seishu responds with stories: sunlit dust at Samish Island that felt like an accomplishment, impatience while waiting for a private interview, and a 2 a.m. cup of tea with no separation from the cup. The last story, from a book about people taking on big barriers, tells of a woman standing in the rain at an antinuclear demonstration, unaware that Dr. Benjamin Spock had driven past and decided to join.

sentences.text: I've become a real fan of Sojun Mel Weitsman ever since Tim gave a talk on the book Umbrella Man, which is about his 80th birthday.
All of Mel's main students, his dharma heirs, wrote a section about what kind of a teacher he was and what they learned from him, what kind of teacher he is, because he's still with us.
I got interested in him and I've looked up some of his talks on the internet, and I've really enjoyed them.

So tonight I'm going to read a talk he gave during a seven day sesshin, and then I'm going to make some comments about just how that talk affects me, and maybe there'll be some time afterwards for discussion.
The name of the talk is called Continuous Practice, How and Why.
*Today is the sixth day of our seven day Rohatsu sesshin.
We have been sitting zazen, that means sitting meditation.
We have been sitting zazen, doing kinhin, walking meditation, eating meals, cooking meals, and serving each other.
Moment after moment we've been dealing with our silent dramas, dealing with our not so silent dramas, with our complaints and our doubts.
This is continuous practice, a very concentrated time of continuous practice.
During this time two questions come up.
One is why and the other is how.
Sesshin is pretty difficult.
Sesshin means a seven day meditation retreat.
Sesshin is pretty difficult.
It's difficult to stay in our seat, dealing with painful legs, painful mind, listening to the loop of our thoughts, continually going round and round.
It's sometimes difficult accepting various emotions that come up.
It's difficult settling ourself on the self without getting caught by emotion, thought, or painful legs, without becoming attached to any nice states of mind which might occasionally occur.
The state of mind one seeks in zazen is no special state of mind.
When we first read about meditation it's very intriguing or lured into this activity, hoping to reach nirvana.
We don't understand that nirvana is the pain in our legs.
Too bad.
So it's natural to look for something special to bring home.*
*We sit here for a week and we say, what happened?
Nothing happened.
It all went by in a moment.
What did I get after seven days?
Nothing.
Just painful legs.
So the sesshin state of mind is no particular state of mind.
What we get is no special thing.
If you get something that might be a mistake.
Be careful.

This is seven days of letting go, seven days of dropping, seven days of non-clinging, seven days of not discriminating, seven days of allowing whatever state of mind is present to be present, seven days of not chasing away evil thoughts, not coveting good thoughts, not grasping wonderful states of mind, not rejecting painful states of mind, just being present with whatever is present.*
*That's all.
The most difficult thing of all is just to stay in your seat.
We're always moving around.
That's our life.
Life doesn't stand still.
We look for the next comfortable position, the next interesting thing.
It's very hard to stay where we are, to stay in our place.
So we have these two questions.
The first is, why do we do this?
When we start to sit, we instinctively know why.
It's beyond our reasoning, but somehow we know.
Knowing knows.
When we start to reason about it, we don't know anymore.
We try to match our reasoning with our knowing, and it brings up the question, especially when we get into a difficult spot.
It's like taking a boat ride.
We know that we enjoy going out on a boat, but then a big storm comes up.
Pretty soon the boat's leaning over, the sails are starting to rip, the waves are coming over the gunnels, and we say, why did we ever do this?
But it doesn't help.
The real question is, how do I deal with this?
How is the practice question.
Why is valid, but it's secondary to how.
Take your life, for example.
Why was I born?
It doesn't matter.
Here you are.
The real question is, how do I live this life?
How do I deal with this situation?
When we hold this question of how, that's continuous practice.
You can deal with why until you get tired of it, and then turn to the how.
How do I do this?
This is the koan of your life.*
*Occasionally someone will ask me, how can I be a good Zen student?
Invariably I say, just keep that question.
It's a great question.
Keep that question in all your activity.
How do I do what's in front of me?
How do I practice moment to moment?
We're not seeking something far off.
We're seeking to know, how do I stand in this place right now?
How do I sit in this spot right now, totally?
This is not just about sitting zazen, but about walking, eating, moving.
How do I harmonize body-mind with the universe?
That's our practice.
When we sit, we harmonize body and mind with the universe without discriminating, without picking and choosing.
How do we harmonize the intellect with the heart?*
*Where is the center of our being?
When we find our center, our heart, then the mind is under control.
If the mind is not under control of the heart, it becomes a divorce from humanity.
It begins to exaggerate its own importance and can become what we call evil.
Comic books are archetypal stories which represent the real battles of our time.
Batman, Superman, Spiderman.
In comic books, there's always an evil one with a big head.
He has all the technical control at his command.
The hero has spiritual strength.
The battle between the head and the heart is actually the battle of our time, between the forces of technology of expanding brain power and the spirit struggling to bring these under control.
The tensions of our time arise because technology and brain power are easily cut off from the heart, from the solar plexus, from the vital center.
In comic books, the hero is always trying to keep it together.
The same battle goes on in each one of us.
How can we keep the mind, the heart, and all the other satellites in harmony?
When the mind is divorced from our vital center, it leads to cunning, to domination and unrest.
The world is in a terrible state of unrest and getting worse all the time.
Zen practice is to harmonize the mind and keep it under control so that it can work in harmony with the heart and the rest of the body.
The mind should be working for humanity, not just for its own satisfaction.*
*We sit up straight, harmonizing all this in one act.
We don't care so much about intellectual speculation.
Instead, we care about being grounded.
Even Buddhist speculation is not so important.
Buddhist philosophy is fine if you're grounded, but the first thing is to be grounded.
The first order of practice is always to be grounded.
When you pick up a cup of tea, pick up the cup with both hands.
Drink the tea with no separation between you and the cup and the tea.
The cup is not an object, the tea is not an object.
There are no objects.
When we let go of everything, no one thing stands out.
The center of yourself is the center of everything.
When we sit zazen, we bring the whole world into harmony.
This is called saving all beings.
Even though people are still out there killing each other, the influence of your continuous practice has far-reaching effects which you can never know.
As long as individuals are out of balance, the world will be out of balance.
In order to bring the world into balance, we start with ourselves.
This is our way of saving beings.
This is what we've been doing all week.*
So that's Mel's talk, and in that short little talk there's a lot of things that stand out for me.

Continuous practice while sitting, walking, eating, taking breaks, going to the bathroom, all the time dealing with a never-ending series of thoughts, emotions, physical sensations, trying to stay grounded, practicing letting go over and over again.
In my case, often realizing that once again I've been caught by nice states of mind or something unpleasant that I've spun into a story.
I've had many sesshins that were primarily emotional and physical turmoil, where it seemed like my mind and body never really settled down.
Either varieties of physical pain or sleepiness, or I just kept getting drawn into thoughts and feelings one after another for seven days.
But even with those sesshins, I've never felt like the time spent was wasted.
I've always been glad that I went and I felt like I got something out of it, even if I couldn't really explain what that something was.
Maybe just a feeling that I did something worth doing, that I tried.
There's something worthwhile in making the effort to settle and stay grounded regardless of the results.
I think this touches on the why do this.
You don't need a good explanation or even good results.
I think we all have the capacity to know what we need in life.
It's a matter of trusting your instincts, trusting your intuition, that something is worthwhile, worth doing, that a certain path is the right path.
I think we all have that in us, the ability to know that, to know when we're on the right path.
Mel talks about what we get is no special thing: *If you get something that might be a mistake.
Be careful.*
During one sesshin at Samish Island a couple years ago, I had a really lovely experience.
It was about the fourth day of meditation.
Everybody was really into the routine of when to get up and when to eat and when to meditate.
Things weren't moving along.
The teacher had just given the instruction, meditate with your ears, which means listen very carefully.
I was unusually focused then.
My mind was very quiet.
In this room we were meditating.
I noticed the sun coming in through a window illuminating dust beams in the air.
It was just beautiful.
I watched it for a while.
I don't know how long.
I think it's the happiest I've ever been in my life.
I was completely joyful just watching little particles of dust illuminated by the sun floating through the air.
I don't know how long that lasted, but I felt like, wow, this is something.
I've accomplished something.
I remember mentioning it to the teacher a day or so later during our private interview.
He said, sometimes these mistakes happen, and then just moved on to another talk.
I was expecting a pat on the back or something.
I didn't get it, so I was disappointed.
I understand better now that meditating with an agenda to accomplish something, or "I've got to get that state of mind again," that's a trap.
Carrying around preferences about what your meditation is supposed to be like or what it's supposed to develop into adds a lot of suffering.
Carrying around likes and dislikes, "I want to have this experience, I don't want to have that," just adds a lot of disappointment to our life.
Better to just try to stay grounded.
Notice, acknowledge, and let go.
I know Norman's made the comment, if you do happen to get enlightened, your reaction would be, oh, that was nice.
Now back to the breath.
Again, back to the article, the emphasis on how do we do this?
How do we live this life?
How do we live this moment?
What's the best way to live this particular moment?
And the next one, and the next one.
It's a great thing to keep in mind and it's one of the things we get to practice when we meditate, whether we meditate for half an hour or whether we meditate for a day or we meditate for a week.
How do I respond to this thought, to this feeling, to this sensation?
*The mind should be working for humanity, not for its own satisfaction.* I heard a song once and I have never forgotten the title.
I think anyone who meditates will notice this title.
The song is called, My Mind Has a Mind of Its Own.
I'm not going to sing it.
But when I heard that, I just immediately thought of meditation and how the mind can just run wild.
My mind so often seems intent on either its own satisfaction or its own distraction or just its own movement from one thing to another.
During one sesshin, I was waiting to have my private talk with the teacher and I had some things I wanted to talk about and I was getting impatient.
When is it going to be my turn?
There was a person going around bringing people to talk to the teacher and I didn't think they were doing it right.
Like, how come they're picking other people and not me?
Instead of noticing my impatience and watching it and not adding to it or reacting to it, I got caught by it and I started to get upset and I started to make it personal.
Why aren't they picking me?
It's just on purpose.
That's just like me as the center of the universe.
Everything that's happening is about me, and that's always a trap and that's always a way to have more suffering.
I probably looked like I was meditating, but I was trying to keep my head still and kind of watching who's getting picked and what's the order and all that kind of stuff.
So I spent a certain amount of time being angry and upset, and then I noticed I started to feel really sad, very sad.
I realized, wow, look at all the pain that you cause yourself and other people when you think this way.
I think the person bringing people to talk to the teacher had no agenda against me and probably was just doing her job.
I made it something personal, and I realize, and I do that sometimes, it's nothing but a way to cause yourself more pain.
So I felt sad for quite a while, and then I almost burst out laughing.
The whole thing just seemed so ridiculous.
What a crazy thing to do, to make a big story, get all upset about it, create all this trouble, and it's all my own doing.
After all that, it was just really interesting to look at the whole thing: the anger, the sadness, the humor, and then on to something else.
This whole story speaks about the mind that is not under control of the heart: *it begins to exaggerate its own importance.* *The first order of practice is always to be grounded.
When you pick up a cup of tea, pick the cup up with both hands, drink the tea with no separation between you and the cup and the tea.
The tea is not an object.
The cup is not an object.
There are no objects.* I've told this story before and it's about tea, but it really fits this part.
Some while back I was having trouble sleeping in the middle of the night, so I got up.
It was probably two in the morning, at my house.
Went downstairs.
I thought, I'm going to be up for a while, I'm not tired, so I'll make a cup of tea.
So I boiled water.
I put a bag in the cup and I poured the water in the kitchen.
Then I picked up the cup and I'm walking back into the living room.
It's completely dark.
The house is completely quiet.
No activity in the neighborhood.
No cars driving by.
Nothing.
And I could feel the warmth of the cup that I'm holding and I could see the steam coming up and I could smell the tea.
I sat down and I took a sip and I could feel, it seemed like I could feel the warmth go all the way into my stomach, and it really tasted good.
It was the best cup of tea I've ever had, and it's the same tea I drink several times a day and I've never had another cup like that.
I'm not sure how that happened, but there was no separation between me and the tea, and it was the best tea I've ever had.
So that's what he's talking about here.
Imagine living like that more often.
Everything matters.
Giving your full attention even to the simplest act.
Everything is alive and a part of you and you are a part of it.
As Mel says, *the center of yourself is the center of everything.*

He talks about *the influence of your continuous practice has far-reaching effects which you can never know.* This reminds me of a story that I read in a book called The Impossible Will Take a Little Longer.
I can't remember the author, but it's a series of stories about people that have taken things on with big barriers and really had some success, and it's a very optimistic book.
In this particular story, a woman talked about joining an anti-nuclear weapons demonstration in Washington D.C. in the early 1960s when the movement was just getting started.
I think she said there were maybe a dozen people and they were standing near a busy street in Washington D.C. in view of the White House, and they were holding signs and it was raining really hard.
She stood out there for several hours and she started to think, you know, what am I doing here?
What's the point of standing in the rain?
There's 10 people here.
People are just driving by.
Nobody's paying any attention.
This isn't really doing anything.
I don't know why I'm bothering.
But she stuck it out.
Then she later found out that, unbeknownst to her, Dr.
Benjamin Spock drove by and saw that particular demonstration and thought, if they can stand out in the rain and hold those signs, I can get involved in this movement too.
I don't know if all of you know him.
I think he's dead now, but he was a pediatrician who wrote some very influential books called Baby and Child Care in the 40s, 50s, 60s, I think even into the 70s.
But he got involved in the anti-nuclear weapons movement and he became very influential and he drew a lot of people in.
So this woman, her presence there and the presence of a few other people inspired him and really brought some momentum to this movement.
So you never know how your activity impacts others.
*When we sit zazen, we bring the world into harmony.
In order to bring the world into balance, we start with ourselves.* And that's what we're doing here.
So thank you for listening.
